articles.title: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat

paras.en: On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days.

Now, the Mars analog astronauts—Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery—have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission.

The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment, so the crew could practice Marswalks.

“For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream, just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

After the speech, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway, who had just completed a mission at the International Space Station, knocked on the door to the Mars habitat, called out “trick or treat” and opened it to reveal the crew’s smiling faces. Since then, the analog astronauts have been participating in post-mission evaluations and debriefs that, along with the data collected during their year in the simulated environment, will help inform future missions to Mars and those closer to home, per a NASA statement.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Most days, we had things that were scheduled, from maintenance and science and engineering activities and some operational activities. So, we often do extravehicular activities, also known as EVAs or spacewalks,” Elder, who was the mission’s commander and test pilot, tells CNN News Central. “We would do drone and rover operations where we control certain equipment outside of the habitat, and we would practice additional data collection for both human health and behavioral sciences.”

Each team member brought unique expertise to the mission. Elder was an experimental test pilot at the U.S. Air Force. Ellis, the mission’s medical officer and tactical thinker, is a U.S. Space Force officer. Spicer was the flight engineer and systems specialist, and he has experience in satellite communications and spacecraft development. Montgomery’s diverse background in hardware engineering, robotics, technology startups and independent films made him the “Swiss Army knife of crewmates;” he served as the mission’s science officer and versatile engineer.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Quick fact: When was the first CHAPEA mission?

The first mission of this kind also lasted 378 days, during which crewmembers Kelly Haston, Ross Brockwell, Nathan Jones and Anca Selariu entered the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on June 25, 2023, and emerged on July 6, 2024.

Elder tells Fox News that combining their skills created “magic.” But that didn’t happen by accident; the selection process lasted about a year and a half and included personality evaluations by NASA psychologists, Montgomery tells the outlet. What’s more, they got to practice before entering the habitat.

“The crew spent a lot of time together prior to the mission, so we got to work on our teamwork and build relationships,” Montgomery tells Nature’s Kaia Glickman, including during a winter camping expedition that overlapped with a blizzard. “These high-pressure scenarios set a nice foundation for pre-training, where we spent five weeks together before going into isolation. Through all of those tools that we built, we had a really good dynamic as a team inside of the habitat, and conflict was very minimal.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Montgomery and his crewmates could still speak with mission control, but the communication system intentionally mimicked delays that would occur on a real Mars mission. That meant messages could take up to 22 minutes to deliver, and the team even had to deal with a planned two-week communication blackout. Future travelers to Mars will experience this communications barrier when Earth and the Red Planet are temporarily on opposite sides of the sun, blocking radio signals from traveling between the planets, according to Nature.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Over the next several years,” Spicer tells Fox News, “the NASA researchers will be going through the data from our mission, as well as the previous CHAPEA mission, to figure out how well we did and what they still need to work on in the coming years to get real people to Mars.”

articles.title: Archaeologists in England Discovered 8,000 Roman-Era Frog Bones in a Single Ditch. They Just Solved the Mystery of How the Amphibians Ended Up There

paras.en: Between 2016 and 2022, archaeologists conducting excavations along a planned stretch of England’s A14 highway unearthed an array of astonishing discoveries, including a Roman amulet carved to resemble the mythical Gorgon Medusa, the earliest physical evidence of beer production in Britain and an Iron Age comb crafted from a human skull.

Comprising more than 280,000 artifacts, the finds—uncovered between modern-day Cambridge and Huntingdon—shed light on life in the region over roughly 12,000 years. But some discoveries raised more questions than answers: Why, for example, did a single ditch at the Bar Hill site in rural Cambridgeshire contain some 8,000 amphibian bones?

As Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA), told the Observer’s Dalya Alberge in 2022, “In my experience, mainly working on sites from London, we don’t get that many frogs. To have so many bones coming from one ditch is extraordinary.”

Ewens and her colleagues outlined several possible explanations for the unusual cache. Perhaps the amphibians fell into the ditch (also described as a gully) and found themselves trapped. Or maybe they succumbed to extreme cold during their wintertime hibernation. Alternatively, they could have served as the centerpiece of a meal—or several—enjoyed by Iron Age humans, although the absence of cut marks on the bones rendered this scenario unlikely.

Four years after MOLA first announced the find, experts have finally solved the mystery of the ancient animal cemetery. Based on a groundbreaking analysis of amphibian arm bones, researchers led by Ewens and Paul Clarkson, an archaeologist at England’s Bournemouth University, concluded that most of the frogs whose remains were found in the ditch died young, eaten by birds of prey such as short-eared owls and hen harriers in the second or third century C.E., during Britain’s Roman era.

A combination of environmental factors and human activity produced ideal conditions for this avian feast to unfold over a relatively short timeframe. As the authors write in the journal Environmental Archaeology, water levels in the Fens—the marshy wetland that houses the gully—retreated during the Roman period, enabling frogs in drying-out ponds to reproduce at a faster rate. When birds in search of their next meal arrived, they had no trouble spotting their prey: Locals had felled the trees in the area to make way for grazing livestock, leaving the amphibians with limited woodland protection from aerial predators.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: - All toads are frogs, but not all frogs are toads. Both animals belong to the Anura order, meaning they are amphibians that lack tails.

- According to the University of Michigan’s Animal Diversity Web database, “There is no scientific distinction between ‘frogs’ and ‘toads,’ although most anurans are usually referred to as one or the other.”

“We don’t often get an owl’s eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” Clarkson says in a statement. “These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world—what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them.”

The majority of the bones belonged to frogs and toads (specifically common frogs), but shrews, voles and mice were also present in the assemblage. The remains represented no fewer than 469 individual animals.

To estimate the frogs’ ages at their time of death, the researchers measured the amphibians’ distal humeri, or arm bones—a method previously described by Clarkson and several co-authors in a 2025 paper. According to the study, the team determined that a large number of the frogs died in either their first or second year of life, during a “short, intensive predation event” spanning autumn to the following spring, “probably along migration routes to and from hibernation sites.” An abundance of frogs likely attracted “local and migrant predators to the area to feed on them and also, coincidentally, on other locally available prey, such as voles, insectivores, birds and fish.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Based on breakage patterns and physical traces of digestion seen on the bones, the paper’s authors ruled out several species that typically prey on amphibians, including otters, gray herons and grass snakes. Instead, they suggest that the “lightly digested and relatively unbroken bones” are more consistent with medium-sized birds such as short-eared owls.

Initially, the archaeologists identified the gully as a roundhouse in an enclosure dating to Britain’s Iron Age, which began around 750 B.C.E. and ended with the Roman invasion in 43 C.E. But radiocarbon dating of the bones shifted this timeline forward by several hundred years.

How did humans fit into this puzzle? Although the researchers considered the possibility that ancient people intentionally deposited the bones in the ditch, the only evidence for this scenario was the presence of a Roman-era brooch among the animal remains. In all likelihood, the authors argue in the paper, the mass predation event only took place because humans weren’t in the area at the time: Short-eared owls “only choose quiet roosting sites, so people must have rarely visited this area, particularly with dogs.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Why locals steered clear of this specific spot in the autumn and winter remains unclear, but the scientists posit that “the most probable explanation is seasonal movement of livestock.” Avoidance tied to social or ritual reasons is also possible.

“I had so many theories as to why such [a] large collection of frog bones were recovered from this small feature,” Ewens says in the statement. “This research shows how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”

articles.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms

paras.en: In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake.

The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm.

“It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young, a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist. “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.”

Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost, or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science.

To better understand what happened, the team homed in on two major events: the Johnson River slide in August 2017 that moved about 4.5 million cubic meters of dirt and rock, and the Redstone River slide in August 2018 that sent roughly 18 million cubic meters of debris tumbling down. Satellite imagery captured between 1980 and 2020 and field studies revealed some odd characteristics, the team found.

“Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope,” Young tells Live Science. “But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris.”

The team monitored the temperature near the 1995 burn area near the slides and, for comparison, undisturbed forest from September 2020 to August 2022. Their data went into computer simulations, which allowed the researchers to investigate how the wildfires decades earlier may have affected the region.

Their resulting hypothesis? The fires that swept through the landscape burned off the vegetation that usually keeps the permafrost cool on sunny days. “After about 20 years or so, that thermal signature from the burned forest can reach the base of permafrost,” Young tells Grist. “It’s slight, but it’s there.”

As the frozen ground warmed, it weakened and formed cracks, allowing water to seep in. That allowed the permafrost to thaw even more, destabilizing its bottom layers. Eventually, that caused the ground to detach and created the two landslides at the center of the study. They’re among more than 150 permafrost landslides in the area that happened around two decades after the severe wildfires, meaning the newly proposed mechanism could have contributed to many of these catastrophic events.

The findings suggest scientists need to better study what’s happening below the surface of permafrost regions, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who wasn’t involved in the work, to Nikk Ogasa at Science News. “We don’t know how [the ground] will move—it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”
Thankfully, Young says experts can look out for signs of an impending permafrost detachment slide and predict when it’s going to happen.

“That’s kind of the silver lining,” he tells Julia Parrish at the CBC. “It doesn’t just happen overnight; it kind of happens in a more progressive manner over the course of about 20 years after a fire, where you get a slow downslope movement of these slopes.”

articles.title: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive
articles.author: Matt Simon

paras.en: The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

articles.title: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets
articles.author: Julian Chokkattu

paras.en: You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.

Kim says everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.

Giving AI a physical body isn't new, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.

OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.

It can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim says, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.

The catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.

Kim says she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.

But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.

It's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic announced a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.
Kim says that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.

“Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim says. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this."

articles.title: Logitech Yeti 2 Review: An All-In-One Studio Setup
articles.author: Henri Robbins

paras.en: The original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.

Long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box. The built-in screen and dial allow for on-the-fly adjustments right on the microphone. No software required. While I was a skeptic at first, I quickly found this little screen to be significantly more convenient than the alternative. It can be used to adjust gain, enable different post-processing settings, and configure the sound profile of the microphone.

More importantly, the screen can quickly provide insights into audio quality at a glance. The main screen shows a graph of the gain-adjusted input volume, which is what the microphone is sending to your computer. It can also display a histogram of volume over time, a pattern to show what direction input is coming from, or … a pixel-art Yeti. This little guy looks confused when you’re quiet, happy when you’re talking at a normal volume, and alarmed when you’re too loud for the microphone to handle. Within the G Hub app, the icons can be swapped out with any of Logi’s other premade avatars (a dragon, flower, frog, or jellyfish), or freely customized with your own images using a simple drag-and-drop menu. This is the least functional feature of the microphone, but it’s an endearing and intuitive way to indicate audio quality at a glance.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The screen also has quite a few adjustable menus for different features, including a de-noise function with four levels, five EQ presets, a pattern customizer with eight default options, and a multitude of toggleable settings to clean up and improve recording quality. While the settings can’t be customized using the screen, the G Hub application provides more in-depth adjustments for how intense each of these settings are, along with explanations of how they work and when to use them.

articles.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
articles.author: Laura Chung and Tatsiana Chypsanava

paras.en: To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife.
Then she sets up a trap along that path.

“We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland.
“We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.”

Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke, a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled.

The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year.
Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer.

articles.title: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
articles.author: Ian Austen

paras.en: The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.
Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.
Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.

“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”

Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

articles.title: Too Many Chips in One Basket?
articles.author: Katrin Bennhold

paras.en: A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.

Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”
But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.

Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”

The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

articles.title: Karol G Postpones Show in Mexico City ‘Due to Health Reasons’: Here’s the New Date
articles.author: Sigal Ratner-Arias

paras.en: The third concert that Karol G was set to perform on Sunday (Nov. 15) at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City, as part of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, has been postponed to Tuesday (Nov. 17) “due to health reasons of the artist,” Ocesa announced on social media.

“This decision has been made prioritizing her health and well-being,” the promoter said in a statement. “After two nights full of music and special moments in Mexico City, we deeply regret not being able to share tonight with all the fans who were looking forward to joining her. Karol G sincerely thanks everyone for the love and energy they have given her these past days and appreciates their understanding at this time.”

Ocesa informed fans that tickets previously purchased for Sunday’s concert will be valid for the new date, so no changes are necessary. Those who wish to request a refund can do so through Ticketmaster.
The specific health issue of the Colombian superstar was not disclosed. Billboard reached out to Karol G’s representatives on Sunday night but did not receive a response at press time.

On Friday (November 13), the “Bichota” singer performed the first of her three concerts at the iconic stadium in Mexico City, where Thalia made a surprise guest appearance to sing a duet of “Piel Morena,” “Amor a la Mexicana” and “¿A Quién Le Importa?” The performance marked the return of the iconic Mexican singer and actress to the stages of Mexico City after a decade.
During her second show on Saturday night (Nov. 14), Karol invited pop star Belinda onstage to perform tracks such as “Luz Sin Gravedad,” “Ángel” and “Bella Traición” together.

As part of the start of the Latin American leg of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, the Colombian singer previously visited the northern Mexican city of Monterrey, where she performed on Nov. 6, 7 and 8 at the Estadio BBVA.
This week, she was also in Las Vegas for the Latin Grammys, taking home awards including best reggaeton performance for “Verano Rosa,” with Feid, and best urban music album for Tropicoqueta.

articles.title: Gracie Abrams Sets 2027 Australian Arena Shows for ‘Look at My Life Tour’
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Gracie Abrams is bringing The Look at My Life Tour to Australia next year.

Abrams will play six arena shows across two cities in July and August 2027: three nights at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena on July 27, 28 and 30, followed by three at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on Aug. 3, 4 and 6. British singer-songwriter Arlo Parks will open all six dates.

“Australia! I’ve missed you so much and I cannot express just how excited I am to return to Melbourne and Sydney next July/August for ‘The Look at My Life Tour,’” Abrams said in a statement. “A show that we’ve been working very hard to put together, a show that we hope you love as much as we do.”

“I’ve just missed you so much more than I can tell you… as soon as I heard for sure we were coming back my heart began to sing,” she added. “I will see you soon, I love you so much… we’re gonna make it great.”

The tour supports Daughter From Hell, Abrams’ third studio album, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in July with 124,000 equivalent album units, her first chart-topping album. Produced with longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner, it also reached No. 1 in Australia. A deluxe edition arrives Friday (Nov. 20) with five additional tracks, including “Out of Nowhere,” which she first performed at Glastonbury in 2025, and “Crazy Girl,” previously available only on vinyl. The Look at My Life Tour launches Dec. 2 in Denver.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The run marks Abrams’ third visit to Australia in four years. She sold out six theater shows on her first trip in January 2024, then returned in 2025 for 11 arena dates across Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth on The Secret of Us Tour. This time she is concentrating on two markets.

The Secret of Us (2024) debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and its deluxe edition produced “That’s So True,” her first top 10 hit on the Billboard Hot 100. Her Taylor Swift collaboration “us.” earned a Grammy nomination for best pop duo/group performance. Abrams will also make her acting debut in the upcoming A24 film Please.

An artist presale begins Wednesday (Nov. 18) at 10 a.m. local time, followed by Frontier Touring and Live Nation presales Thursday (Nov. 19). General sale opens Friday (Nov. 20) at 10 a.m. local time.

articles.title: Watch Olivia Dean, Kehlani, Juanes & More Revealing 2027 Grammy Nominations Here
articles.author: Paul Grein

paras.en: UPDATE: This story has been updated with the livestream where you can watch the nominations be unveiled, starting at 7:45 a.m. ET on Monday (Nov. 16).

Olivia Dean, the reigning Grammy winner for best new artist, is widely expected to receive multiple Grammy nominations, including album, record and song of the year, on Monday, Nov. 16. She’s also set to help announce the nominations on a livestream bright and early that morning, along with Kehlani, who won two Grammys earlier this year and could be in line for more awards for her eponymous album; Amy Allen, who has won songwriter of the year, non-classical the last two years; and Pharrell Williams, a past three-time winner of producer of the year, non-classical.

Nominees across all 100 categories for the 2027 Grammys will be revealed during a special presentation on Grammy.com and the Grammys YouTube channel, with special live coverage on Good Morning America. The nominations livestream begins on Monday, Nov. 16 at 7:45 a.m. ET / 4:45 a.m. PT. There will be a wrap-up show at 9 a.m. ET/6 a.m. PT (times approximate).
For the first time, the Grammy Nominations special presentation will be broadcast live at The Square in Times Square, presented by Hilton.
The complete nominations list will be published on Grammy.com and at Billboard.com at 9 a.m. ET / 6 a.m. PT.

The Grammys also made an important announcement about the 2027 Grammys, which will air one hour earlier than in the past. The 69th annual Grammy Awards will air/stream live on Sunday Feb. 7, 2027 at 7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT on ABC, and stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

This follows the lead of the Oscars, which first moved up their show to start at 4 p.m. PT for the 96th Academy Awards in 2024. The move is designed to allow viewers on the East Coast to remain with the show for the top awards without having to stay up to midnight. 2024 was Raj Kapoor’s first year as an executive producer of the Oscars. Kapoor is also an executive producer of the Grammys.
The 2027 Grammys will again be held at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Russell Brand Says He’s “Not Guilty” in Message From Prison Read By His Wife: “Something Strange Is Happening”
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Russell Brand has shared a message from prison, delivered by his wife, Laura Brand, on his YouTube channel Sunday.

“So Russell has asked me to read something to you today,” she said at the beginning of the video, before looking to a notebook to read her husband’s message. “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault last Monday. The trial lasted four weeks at Southwark Crown Court, with the jury finding him guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault (he was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault).

Laura continued to deliver Russell’s message, reading, “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders prison in Europe.’ The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.”

“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us. Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers. Your brother in Christ, Russell,” the remarks concluded.
In a pre-recorded portion of the YouTube video, Russell compared the coverage of his trial to that of a “football match.”

“So obviously, as I said last week, we’re in the middle of a trial,” he said. “I mean, we don’t really look at coverage, but someone showed me some of the coverage the other day from people that were actually broadly supportive. But I know that’s not generally how it’s being covered in the mainstream media, and you can draw your own conclusions from that. Although what I will say is, it’s amazing to watch other people’s coverage of it because they just talk about it like it’s a football match.”
In a new report from The Times and Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret documentary, six more women accused of him of alleged sexual misconduct.
Read The Hollywood Reporter‘s deep dive into the years-long road to Russell’s sentencing here.

articles.title: Governors Awards: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman Accept Honorary Oscars, Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler Receive Thalberg Award
articles.author: Scott Feinberg

paras.en: Five giants of the global film community were feted on Sunday night at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ 17th annual Governors Awards: actress Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman and — in absentia due to a recent medical procedure — director/producer Ridley Scott with bestowed honorary Oscars, and longtime indie producing partners Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, which recognizes “creative producers whose bodies of work reflect a consistently high quality of motion picture production.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The black-tie gathering, which took place inside the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, was, as always, packed with Academy members — including most of the 55 members of the organization’s board of governors, who host the event — and dozens of current Oscar contenders. Among them: You Can See Everything’s Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, The Odyssey’s Christopher Nolan, Zendaya, Tom Holland and Charlize Theron, The Debut’s Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti and Emma Stone, Obsession’s Curry Barker and Inde Navarrette, La Bola Negra’s Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, Elsinore’s Andrew Scott, The Invite’s Olivia Wilde and Penélope Cruz, Wild Horse Nine’s John Malkovich, Artificial’s Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, and Dune: Part Three’s Timothée Chalamet, accompanied by Kylie Jenner.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Seated with Scott were his family, along with Lucy Fisher, Doug Wick, Jim Gianopulos, Tom Rothman, Richard Lovett, Simon Halls, Steve Asbell, Matt Damon and Jerry Bruckheimer, while

Norman was notably joined by Marlon West and Travon Free. Close’s table consisted of Malkovich, Kevin Huvane, Franklin Latt, Rodrigo Garcia and Ram Bergman. Vachon and Koffler were accompanied by John Sloss, Wash Westmoreland, Marcus Hu and Liz Karlsen.

The first awardee was Norman, 91, who began his career in 1956 at Walt Disney Animation Studios as the company’s first Black animator. He contributed to numerous Disney classics including Sleeping Beauty, The Sword in the Stone, Mary Poppins, The Jungle Book and Robin Hood, as well as other notable films made outside of the Mouse House including The Hunchback of Notre Dame, Mulan, Monsters, Inc. and Toy Story 2. A friend and mentor to younger animators and storyboard artists, he was the subject of a 2016 documentary feature, Floyd Norman: An Animated Life.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Norman — only the fourth animator to ever receive that accolade, after Walter Lantz, Chuck Jones and Hayao Miyazaki — was led by Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali, who stated, “Floyd has played a pivotal role in our lives without any of us even realizing it, one [animation] cel at a time.”

In his acceptance speech, Norman reflected on his beginnings in the industry, offering “a special thank you to the best mentor a filmmaker could ever have, Walt Disney.” He concluded his speech remarking, “On occasion, even movies have a happy ending. This special evening? Here’s my happy ending.”

The evening’s next honoree was Close, one of the great stars and character actresses of the past 50 years. The 79-year-old has received eight Oscar nominations, four for leading performances (1987’s Fatal Attraction, 1988’s Dangerous Liaisons, 2011’s Albert Nobbs and 2018’s The Wife) and four for supporting turns (1982’s The World According to Garp, 1983’s The Big Chill, 1984’s The Natural and 2020’s Hillbilly Elegy). She could just as easily have been nominated for 1985’s Jagged Edge and Maxie, 1990’s Reversal of Fortune, 1994’s The Paper, 1996’s 101 Dalmatians and 1997’s Air Force One.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Close’s tally of eight noms for performances is higher than that of all but three other actresses, dead or alive — Meryl Streep (21), Katharine Hepburn (12) and Bette Davis (11), each of whom won multiple times — and more than any other living man or woman (Peter O’Toole, who died in 2013, also went 0-for-eight and received an honorary Oscar).

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Close — who previously presented honorary Oscars to the National Endowment for the Arts in 1985, Deborah Kerr in 1994 and Carol Littleton in 2023 — was kicked off by John Malkovich, who described her as “my friend and treasured colleague.” Close’s Dangerous Liaisons co-star then went on to state, “She is a true master… she’s got the goods, she can do the big stuff, the little stuff, and everything in between… Glenn is unafraid to ‘go there,’ and I love that about her,” Malkovich added. “She loves the world, she is relentless, very smart, a little cagey and a great actress who knows exactly what she’s doing and gives it 100 percent every single time.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Following a lengthy standing ovation, Close, who dedicated the award to her daughter, Annie, declared: “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance. I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room. Over the past 43 years, I’ve been in the room eight times… so to be in this room tonight, embraced by the people who have consistently inspired me, whose work has sustained and challenged me and only made me want to be better is the greatest honor of all.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Next up was Scott, whose films, collectively, have been nominated for 45 Oscars and won nine, but who himself has never won a competitive Oscar. The 88-year-old, who was nearly 40 when he made his directorial debut, has made up — and continues to make up — for lost time, consistently pumping out action-packed blockbusters, many now considered landmarks of cinematic achievement.

Indeed, he is behind two of the most significant sci-fi films of all time, 1979’s Alien and 1982’s Blade Runner, as well as 1991’s Thelma & Louise (for which he received a best director Oscar nom), 2000’s Gladiator (which won the best picture Oscar, while he lost best director), 2001’s Black Hawk Down (for which he received his most recent best director Oscar nom) and 2015’s The Martian. He has also produced many of his films, as well as a ton of TV series.

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Scott was led by Matt Damon, who described him as “a master at the helm” of two films they’ve made together, The Martian and The Last Duel, stating, “Thank you to the Academy on behalf of everyone who has ever worked with Ridley Scott. It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand.” Scott accepted his Oscar via a pre-recorded video from London, which included a clip from his first movie, Boy in a Bicycle, featuring his late brother, Tony, in which the narrator states, “I’ll remember this moment when I’m 80, and it’ll all seem like yesterday.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “That was a moment for both of us,” Scott stated. “Now I’m well past 80, and I’ve thought about those days and moments. It does resonate just like yesterday. Both of us sharing our first film together that led to 20 years of advertising, five decades of filmmaking… I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony. His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

The final awardees of the night were Vachon, 63, and Koffler, 60, two of the most important producers in the history of American independent film. The co-founders of New York-based Killer Films have guided to fruition all 10 of Todd Haynes’ features — including Poison (1991), Safe (1995), Far from Heaven (2002) and Carol (2015) — plus Larry Clark’s Kids (1995), Todd Solondz’s Happiness (1998), Kimberly Peirce’s Boys Don’t Cry (1999), John Cameron Mitchell’s Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001), Wash Westmoreland and Richard Glatzer’s Still Alice (2014) and Celine Song’s Past Lives (2023, for which they received their sole Oscar noms).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Vachon, the more public-facing of the duo, has been nicknamed “the Queen of New Queer Cinema” and is such a fixture of the indie scene that she was affectionately referenced alongside Spike Lee, Michael Moore and Richard Linklater in the title of the classic 1996 tome Spike, Mike, Slackers, & Dykes: A Guided Tour Across a Decade of American Independent Cinema. Her own 2006 book A Killer Life, which she co-wrote with Austin Bunn, was included on The Hollywood Reporter‘s 2023 list of the 100 greatest film books of all time.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The presentation of the Thalberg to Vachon and Koffler was kicked off by Neil Patrick Harris with a performance from Hedwig and the Angry Inch, which Vachon and Koffler produced. Todd Haynes and Julianne Moore then conducted the actual handoff of the statuettes, with Haynes saying, “From the outside, they couldn’t see more different, and of course they are. But the ways they trade and riff off each other, divide and share their unique abilities. It’s a shimmering example of how the world might actually be if it were run by adults, otherwise known as women.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Added Moore, “These women have never been driven by profit and even recently admitted to me that no matter how hard they tried to be commercial, they’ve had to make peace of the fact that they’re just not. That doesn’t mean that they haven’t had commercial success. They are just not driven by it. They are interested in radical voices, queer voices, new voices, personal points of view.”

Vachon, in her acceptance speech, dedicated the pair’s honor to their “fellow hardworking producers,” stating, as she recalled a recent interaction, “A producer came up to me in New York and said, ‘I know this is really your Oscar, but it kind of feels like all of ours,’ And it is.”

articles.title: Dystopian Thriller ‘The Flaw’ Is a Cinematic Puzzle About Totalitarianism: “Each One of Us Is a Regime”
articles.author: Georg Szalai

paras.en: In a dark, dystopian future, the Regime decides who belongs and who doesn’t. And the Regime puts the cold and calculating Interrogator on a man who becomes the Suspect to prove his guilt. He puts a ruthless plan of psychological manipulation into action. But could there be a shortcoming in the master plan?

The dystopian thriller The Flaw, a Greece–Latvia co-production, is based on Antonis Samarakis’ novel of the same name, which is a modern Greek classic and bestseller. It is also writer-director Theophilos Papastylianos’ (Algorhythm, Showtime) feature debut, and it is about to get its world premiere, appropriately in the Baltics. The film will debut in the Baltic Film Competition of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

British talent leads The Flaw, with David Dawson, who plays Derek Jarman in Elsinore, portraying the Interrogator, and Arthur McBain (After the Flood, Napoleon) playing the Suspect. Also part of the ensemble cast are Ralf Little, Angela Brouskou, Lyne Renée, Sarah Akokhia and Georgia Small. Thodoris Zacharakis is the cinematographer, while Yannis Chalkiadakis is the editor. Produced by Panos Papahadzis and Papastylianos, the co-producers are Alise Rogule and Lina Yannopoulou. Jacques Kruger is the sales agent.
